title: My Kids FORGOT My 80th Birthday. A Waitress at the Diner Didn't

scenes.text: Sweetheart, on my eightieth birthday, in December of two thousand twenty-four, nobody called. Not my daughter. Not my son. Not one of my grandchildren. I sat by the phone until noon in my good blue dress. Then I put on my coat, drove to the diner on Lexington Avenue, and ordered a slice of pie, alone. And a young waitress I'd never met noticed something nobody else in my life had noticed that day.
scenes.query: elderly woman alone in diner booth
scenes.caption: NOBODY CALLED

scenes.text: Tonight I'm going to tell you what that waitress did, and what I found out about her life a week later, that made me get in my car and drive across town at nine o'clock at night. And what my children said when they finally remembered. Stay with me, honey, because that girl is sitting at my Christmas table now.
scenes.query: Christmas table with empty chair
scenes.caption: AT MY CHRISTMAS TABLE

scenes.text: I want you to understand, honey, I don't blame my children. Not really. Susan lives in Arizona now, with her husband, and she was busy with her own grandbabies that month. Mark was working double shifts before Christmas. Everybody had a lot going on. But eighty is a big number, sweetheart. I'd only get to turn eighty once. And I'd been looking forward to that phone ringing for weeks.
scenes.query: old telephone on side table by window
scenes.caption: EIGHTY ONLY ONCE

scenes.text: I got up early and did my hair. I put on the blue dress Harold bought me for our fortieth anniversary, the one I only wear for church and funerals. I made a pot of coffee and set out two cups, in case anybody stopped by. And I sat in Harold's chair by the window, with the phone in my lap, and I waited. Eight o'clock. Nine. Ten. The mailman came. Just bills and a seed catalog.
scenes.query: two coffee cups on kitchen table morning
scenes.caption: TWO CUPS JUST IN CASE

scenes.text: At eleven, the phone rang, and my heart jumped right out of my chest. It was a man asking if I wanted to extend the warranty on my car. I'm ashamed to say I talked to him for six minutes, honey, just to have somebody to talk to. He was very polite. At noon, I hung up the blue dress, put on my slacks, and I said out loud to Harold's picture, well, Harold, I guess it's just you and me.
scenes.query: elderly woman holding phone disappointed
scenes.caption: JUST YOU AND ME

scenes.text: I want to tell you something about being old, honey, because nobody tells you. It isn't the aches. You get used to the aches. It's the quiet. The phone doesn't ring as much. The Christmas cards get fewer every year, because your friends are passing. Evelyn was gone, and Helen had moved to her daughter's in Florida. And some days, the only voice you hear is the television. I'll tell you how I broke that quiet in a minute.
scenes.query: quiet living room with television on
scenes.caption: IT'S THE QUIET

scenes.text: Harold and I used to go to the Main Street Diner every Saturday for forty years, until it closed. So I drove to the other one, on Lexington Avenue, where nobody knew me. I sat in a booth in the back, by the window, with the Christmas lights blinking outside. And I ordered a cup of coffee and a slice of coconut cream pie. Harold's favorite. In a minute I'll tell you who brought it.
scenes.query: slice of coconut cream pie on diner table
scenes.caption: HAROLD'S FAVORITE

scenes.text: Her name tag said Jasmine. She was about twenty-five, with tired eyes and a pencil stuck in her ponytail, and she was running the whole floor by herself, because the other girl had called in sick. Twelve tables, sweetheart, a week before Christmas. But when she brought my pie, she stopped. She looked at me a little too long. And she said, ma'am, are you okay? You look like you're waiting for somebody.
scenes.query: young tired waitress with pencil in ponytail
scenes.caption: WAITING FOR SOMEBODY

scenes.text: If you're enjoying Grandma's story, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these stories. I said, oh, I'm fine, honey. It's just my birthday. And she said, how old? And I don't know why, but I told her the truth. I said, eighty. And nobody remembered. And then I was crying, in a diner, in front of a stranger, with coconut pie in front of me. Eighty years old.
scenes.query: elderly woman crying softly in diner booth
scenes.caption: NOBODY REMEMBERED

scenes.text: Jasmine didn't say a word, honey. She just walked away. And I thought, well, I've embarrassed that poor girl. But five minutes later, the kitchen door swung open, and here she came with a whole coconut cream pie, not a slice, a whole pie, with one tall candle stuck in the middle, already lit. And behind her came the cook, a big man in an apron, and the dishwasher, a boy about sixteen.
scenes.query: waitress carrying whole pie with lit candle
scenes.caption: A WHOLE PIE

scenes.text: And Jasmine stood in the middle of that diner, with her twelve tables, and she said, real loud, everybody, this is Ruth, and she's eighty today. And she started singing Happy Birthday. And the cook sang. And the dishwasher sang. And a table of truck drivers sang. And a young couple with a baby sang. And by the end, sweetheart, the whole diner was singing to me. Twenty-two strangers.
scenes.query: whole diner singing happy birthday
scenes.caption: TWENTY-TWO STRANGERS

scenes.text: I blew out that candle and made a wish. The truck drivers paid for my pie. The young couple sent their little girl over with a paper napkin she'd drawn a flower on. And Jasmine sat down in my booth for five whole minutes, in the middle of the lunch rush, and asked me about my life. About Harold. About the blue dress. Nobody had asked me about my life in a very long time.
scenes.query: little girl giving drawn flower napkin
scenes.caption: ASKED ABOUT MY LIFE

scenes.text: When I told her about Harold, she put her hand on mine. She said, my grandma used to say the same thing about my grandpa. That he fixed everything with duct tape and a prayer. I asked where her grandma was. She said, she passed last winter, Miss Ruth. In a nursing home in Columbus. And I didn't get to see her at the end, because I couldn't get off work. Nobody was with her. That's why I noticed you.
scenes.query: young woman holding elderly woman's hand
scenes.caption: THAT'S WHY I NOTICED

scenes.text: So far, the empty phone, the blue dress, a whole diner singing, and a waitress with tired eyes. When I went to pay for my coffee, I tried to leave Jasmine fifty dollars. She wouldn't take it. She pushed it back across the counter and said, Miss Ruth, this one's on me. And I saw her face, honey, when she said it. Like fifty dollars was a lot of money to her. Like she really needed it. Stay with me.
scenes.query: money pushed back across diner counter
scenes.caption: THIS ONE'S ON ME

scenes.text: I slipped it under the napkin dispenser anyway, when she wasn't looking. And I went back the next Saturday, and the one after that. Jasmine always gave me the booth by the window, and always had coconut pie waiting. And on the third Saturday, she wasn't there. The cook told me she'd called in. He said, quietly, I think she's getting evicted, Ruth. She's got a little boy. Four years old.
scenes.query: diner cook talking quietly at counter
scenes.caption: GETTING EVICTED

scenes.text: I asked the cook for her address, honey. He hesitated. Then he wrote it on a guest check. It was an apartment building on the east side, the kind with the stairs outside and half the lights burned out. And that night, at nine o'clock, I put on my coat, and I drove over there, eighty years old, in the dark, in the snow. Harold would have had a fit.
scenes.query: old apartment building stairs at night snow
scenes.caption: IN THE DARK SNOW

scenes.text: Jasmine opened the door in her socks, with a little boy hanging on her leg, and boxes all over the floor behind her. She was packing. She said, Miss Ruth? What are you doing here? And I said, honey, how much? She started to say it was fine, and I said, Jasmine. You sang to me when my own children forgot. How much? She said, eleven hundred dollars. Two months behind.
scenes.query: young mother with little boy in doorway boxes
scenes.caption: HOW MUCH?

scenes.text: Her boy's father had left the year before. Her car had broken down in October, and she'd missed two weeks of shifts. She'd been working doubles ever since, and she was still behind. She'd been too proud to ask anybody, sweetheart. Just like me, sitting by that phone. I wrote her a check right there, on top of a moving box. And that little boy, his name was Eli, climbed right up into my lap.
scenes.query: elderly woman writing check on cardboard box
scenes.caption: TOO PROUD TO ASK

scenes.text: Before I left, I told her, honey, I'm not giving you this. I'm paying back twenty-two strangers. And she laughed and cried at the same time. I came back the next morning with a casserole and a bag of groceries, and I helped her unpack all those boxes. Eli showed me every one of his toy trucks, one by one, all forty of them. Stay with me, honey, because my phone finally rang.
scenes.query: little boy showing toy trucks on floor
scenes.caption: FORTY TOY TRUCKS

scenes.text: Three days after my birthday, Susan called, honey. She was crying so hard I could barely understand her. She'd seen the date on a Christmas card she was writing to me, and she'd realized. Then she called Mark, and Mark called me twenty minutes later, crying too. My big, strong son. They kept saying, Mom, how could we forget? How could we forget you were eighty?
scenes.query: middle aged woman crying on phone
scenes.caption: HOW COULD WE FORGET?

scenes.text: And I told them, honey, I'll tell you the truth. It hurt. It hurt more than I'd let anybody know. But I said, I wasn't alone. A girl named Jasmine sang to me, and so did twenty-one other people. And I told them the whole story. And there was a long silence on the line. And then Mark said, Mom, I'm going to call you every Sunday. And he has. Every Sunday since. He hasn't missed one.
scenes.query: elderly woman smiling on phone at kitchen table
scenes.caption: EVERY SUNDAY SINCE

scenes.text: That Christmas, I asked Jasmine and Eli to come to dinner on Maple Drive. Susan flew in from Arizona, which she hadn't done in three years. Mark and his family came. And when Jasmine walked in with a coconut cream pie she'd made herself, Susan hugged her for a long time and whispered thank you, for being there when I wasn't. Jasmine cried. So did Susan. So did I, honey.
scenes.query: family Christmas dinner young mother with pie
scenes.caption: THANK YOU FOR BEING THERE

scenes.text: That was two years ago, sweetheart. Jasmine's going to nursing school now, at night. Eli calls me Grandma Ruth, and he's six, and he's already beaten me at checkers. Every Saturday, I still sit in the booth by the window. And on my birthday this year, my phone started ringing at seven in the morning. Susan, Mark, every grandchild. And Jasmine and Eli showed up at my door with a whole coconut pie and one tall candle.
scenes.query: elderly woman and young boy playing checkers
scenes.caption: ONE TALL CANDLE

scenes.text: Here's what I want you to remember, honey. Call your grandmother. Today. Don't wait for her birthday. And if you ever see an old woman alone in a diner, waiting for somebody, sit down for five minutes. Tell me in the comments, sweetheart, when did you last call your grandma? There are more of my family's stories in the playlist right there on your screen. Good night. Merry Christmas.
scenes.query: diner booth with pie and lit candle
scenes.caption: CALL YOUR GRANDMA
